title: Why do airplane windows have round corners?
question: Why does every opening in an airliner's cabin have rounded corners?
answer: In 1954 two de Havilland Comets broke apart in flight; water-tank tests showed metal fatigue cracks starting at the corner of a square cut-out in the roof. Sharp corners pile up stress on every pressurised flight; rounded corners spread it.
people_rule: People are anonymous representative passengers, crew and engineers. Never a real victim's face, never invented dialogue.

c1.text: On 10 January 1954 the de Havilland Comet G-ALYP broke up in flight off the island of Elba; all 35 people aboard died.
sources: Migflug, 'De Havilland Comet: First, Beautiful, Deadly', https://migflug.com/afterburner/de-havilland-comet-first-jet-airliner-metal-fatigue-square-windows/
Time, 'Science: The Fate of Yoke Peter', https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,823674,00.html

c2.text: On 8 April 1954, about three months later, Comet G-ALYY broke up in flight near Naples.

c3.text: Investigators put a whole Comet in a water tank and pressurised it again and again; it failed from metal fatigue after the equivalent of about 3,000 flights.
sources: Wikipedia, 'BOAC Flight 781' (G-ALYU tank test, equivalent of 3,000 flights), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOAC_Flight_781

Engineers Ireland, 'Beyond the limits of imagination: what do the Comet aircraft failures teach us', https://www.engineersireland.ie/Engineers-Journal/Mechanical/beyond-the-limits-of-imagination-what-do-the-comet-aircraft-failures-teach-us

c4.text: The inquiry traced the failure to the forward ADF (radio direction-finder antenna) window, a cut-out in the roof, not a passenger window.
sources: Wikipedia, 'BOAC Flight 781' (inquiry: failure 'at the forward ADF window in the roof'), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOAC_Flight_781
Migflug, 'The de Havilland Comet: The Beautiful Jet That Taught Us How Aircraft Break', https://migflug.com/jetflights/de-havilland-comet-metal-fatigue-square-windows-investigation-1954/

c5.text: A pressurised cabin is loaded on every flight; stress concentrates at sharp corners of openings and is spread by rounded corners.

scenes.say: This jet is about to break apart.

image.subject: the cabin of a 1950s de Havilland Comet jet airliner in flight, 1954
image.show: a young woman in 1950s travelling clothes at a window seat beside a large, nearly square cabin window with tight corners (not oval), smiling softly at bright clouds outside, other passengers reading behind her, warm afternoon light, calm and unaware

scenes.motion: the young woman watches the clouds with a soft smile and slowly turns her head a little toward the window; bright clouds drift slowly past outside; a passenger behind her turns a page of his newspaper; the cabin vibrates very slightly

scenes.say: January 1954, off the island of Elba. A de Havilland Comet breaks up in mid-air. All thirty-five people on board are lost.

image.subject: a 1950s jet airliner breaking apart in the dusk sky over the Mediterranean, seen at middle distance as a dark silhouette against a burning orange sky; clean smooth wings with nothing hanging under them, no engine pods, no propellers
image.show: the fuselage torn in two mid-air, the front section separating, burning fragments and long smoke trails falling toward the dark sea, an island on the horizon, seen from very far away, small figures on a coastal terrace in the foreground staring up in shock, no bodies, no close-up

scenes.motion: the two halves of the jet drift further apart in the sky and fall slowly toward the sea, burning fragments tumble down trailing long smoke; the small figures on the terrace freeze, one raises a hand to her mouth, another points up; seen from far away, no close-up of the plane

scenes.say: Three months later, near Naples, it happens again.

image.subject: an empty 1950s airport departure gate at night
image.show: rain on a tall window, a single unclaimed suitcase on a bench, a jet's lights fading into the dark sky outside, lonely blue light

scenes.motion: rain streams down the tall window in thin rivulets; the distant jet lights outside fade slowly into the dark; the suitcase on the bench stays still; the room is quiet and empty

scenes.say: So engineers sink a whole Comet in a giant water tank, and pressurise it again and again, flight after flight.

image.subject: a huge 1950s test hall with a complete jet airliner fuselage inside an enormous water tank
image.show: three engineers in shirtsleeves and ties on a gantry above the water, one checking a pressure gauge, cold industrial light, the fuselage half submerged

scenes.motion: the water level in the tank rises slowly around the half-submerged fuselage with small ripples spreading across the surface; one engineer taps the pressure gauge and its needle climbs; the other two lean on the railing and watch the fuselage

scenes.say: About three thousand flights later, the metal tears open. At a corner.

image.subject: the aluminium skin of a 1950s airliner fuselage
image.show: a jagged fatigue crack running out from the sharp corner of a small square opening, riveted skin around it, an engineer's gloved hand and a torch light pointing at the crack, muted red glow on the crack

scenes.motion: the jagged crack grows outward from the sharp corner of the square opening in two or three short sudden jumps; the red glow on the crack pulses; the torch beam and the gloved hand stay steady

scenes.say: Not a passenger window, as the story often goes. A small square opening in the roof, for a radio antenna.

image.subject: the top of a 1950s de Havilland Comet jet airliner fuselage, seen from directly above, looking straight down onto the roof just behind the cockpit
image.show: the long silver roof of the fuselage running up the frame, a small square opening with sharp corners cut into the centre line of the roof on top of the plane, outlined and glowing in red; the oval passenger windows are only a thin row along the far left and right edges, far from the red square; blue sky and clouds below

scenes.motion: the red square opening on the roof pulses softly with a red glow; white clouds slide slowly past far below the plane; the plane itself stays steady and rigid

scenes.say: Every flight, the cabin swells like a balloon. Stress piles up at sharp corners. Round ones spread it out.

image.subject: two openings side by side in a sheet of aircraft metal, one square with sharp corners, one with rounded corners
image.show: glowing amber stress flow lines bending around both openings, crowding into bright red hot spots at the square corners, flowing smoothly around the rounded one

scenes.motion: the glowing amber flow lines stream steadily from top to bottom around both openings; at the sharp corners of the square opening the lines crowd together and the red hot spots glow brighter and brighter; around the rounded opening the lines flow smoothly and stay calm amber

scenes.say: That's why the window next to you has round corners. Nothing is ordinary when you understand how it works.

image.subject: a modern airliner cabin window with rounded corners at golden hour
image.show: a traveller today resting a hand near the window, looking out at a sunset above the clouds, quiet and safe

scenes.motion: the traveller rests a hand near the window and smiles softly while watching the sunset; the clouds outside drift slowly; warm light shimmers gently on the window frame
